title: SAE features sorted by lens kurtosis
takeaway: Nine example SAE features, three per row, show what the lens-kurtosis statistic picks out. High-κ features split into two kinds: ones that name an abstract concept the model is not currently uttering, and ones that push a specific next token. Low-κ features are syntactic bookkeeping whose lens readouts bear no relation to their apparent meaning.
walkthrough:
The item is a grid of feature cards, three examples in each of three rows. Each card reports one [[sparse-autoencoder]] feature. It gives the feature's auto-interpretation label, a short automatically written description of what the feature appears to mean. It gives the feature's [[lens-kurtosis]] $\kappa$. It gives the vocabulary tokens the [[jacobian-lens]] reads most strongly off that feature's decoder direction. And it gives text excerpts on which the feature activates, with the activating tokens highlighted.

$\kappa$ is the statistic that sorts the rows. A feature's decoder direction is pushed through the lens, which yields a score for every token in the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]]. The excess [[kurtosis]] of that score distribution measures how sharply peaked it is, with a Gaussian scoring zero. High $\kappa$ means the direction loads onto a handful of [[j-lens-vector]]s; low $\kappa$ means it spreads diffusely across the vocabulary. Because the [[j-space]] is a [[sparse-subframe]] rather than a subspace, alignment with a small set of lens vectors is the paper's criterion for being in it.

The top row holds [[workspace-features]]: high $\kappa$, naming an abstract concept, active whenever that concept is invoked. The middle row holds [[motor-features]]: also high $\kappa$, but firing immediately before the model utters the token in question. The paper separates the two by a rule. A feature counts as motor when, over its strongest activations, the actual next token sits in its top ten lens tokens more than 10% of the time. The bottom row holds low-$\kappa$ [[bookkeeping-features]].

The worked example is the top-left card, labelled "numeric constraints and ranges", at $\kappa = 20.9$, the 99.9th percentile of the feature distribution. Its top lens tokens are limits, 限, Limit, lím and limit: one concept in several surface forms and languages. Its activating contexts invoke limits — "strictly positive," "in the range of 0, 1," "restricted by a half-plane" — at positions where the model is not about to write the word. That is the shape the paper wants for a [[verbalizable-representation]]: a concept held in a form the model could say, but is not saying.

The bottom row cuts the other way. A loop variable in a decrementing for-loop scores $\kappa = 0.3$, the first digit of a page range in an academic citation scores $\kappa = 0.5$, and a markdown section header scores $\kappa = 0.3$. For each, the top lens tokens are unrelated to the label. The evidence in this figure is illustrative rather than statistical: nine selected cards, with the distributional claim left to the next figure.

terms.definition: One entry in a sparse autoencoder's learned dictionary: a direction in the residual stream that the SAE uses, together with an activation coefficient, to reconstruct activations as a sparse sum. Each card in the figure is one such feature.
The vector an SAE writes back into the residual stream when a feature fires. It is the direction the paper projects through the J-lens to compute that feature's κ.

The figure's sorting statistic: the excess kurtosis of the vocabulary-score distribution obtained by pushing a feature's decoder direction through the J-lens. It measures how sharply the lens reads that direction, relative to a Gaussian.
A distribution statistic for heavy tails and peakedness, defined so that a Gaussian scores zero. Here it is applied not to data but to a score vector over the vocabulary.

Applying the Jacobian lens to a direction produces a score for every vocabulary token; the top-scoring tokens are printed on each card. They stand for what the model would be disposed to say if that direction were present in the residual stream.

The paper's readout method, which assigns each vocabulary token a residual-stream direction encoding the model's potential to verbalize that token. The figure uses it to interpret SAE feature directions.
The single direction the lens associates with one vocabulary token at one layer. A high-κ feature is one whose decoder direction lies close to a small number of these.

The region of activation space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors, which the paper argues behaves like a global workspace. κ is the statistic used to ask whether a given SAE feature lies in it.

The paper's formal description of the J-space: a set of vectors that need not be linearly independent, restricted to sparse combinations. Because of this, closeness to a few lens vectors, rather than membership in a linear subspace, is the test for being in the J-space.

The short natural-language description of a feature's apparent meaning, generated automatically rather than written by the authors. It is the heading of each card, and phrases such as "numeric constraints and ranges" are examples.

Excerpts of text on which the feature fires most strongly, with the specific token positions that trigger it marked. They are the evidence for what a feature responds to, as opposed to what it promotes.

High-κ features that name an abstract concept and activate whenever that concept is invoked in context, without the model being about to say it. These are the features the paper treats as living in the workspace.

High-κ features that activate immediately before, and promote, the utterance of a particular token. They share the high-κ signature with workspace features, which is why the paper calls high κ necessary but not sufficient for workspace membership.

Low-κ features, typically syntactic or surface-level bookkeeping, whose top lens tokens bear no relation to their auto-interpretation label. The paper takes them as the expected inventory of representations that are not in a workspace.
The auto-interpretation label of the top-left card, the figure's worked example of a workspace feature. It fires on text that invokes bounds or ranges.

The top J-lens readout tokens of the "numeric constraints and ranges" feature. They are the same concept in several surface forms and languages, which is the paper's evidence that the feature encodes a concept rather than a string.

terms.term: "strictly positive," "in the range of 0, 1," "restricted by a half-plane"
terms.definition: Activating contexts printed for that feature. Each invokes the idea of a limit, and at none of them is the model about to output the word "limit."
One of the low-κ bottom-row examples: a feature that tracks the loop variable of a for-loop that counts downward. Its lens tokens are unrelated to loops.
Another low-κ example: a feature for the first digit of a page range inside an academic citation. It is bookkeeping about text layout rather than a nameable concept.
The third low-κ example: a feature for markdown section headers in academic papers. Like the other two, its lens readout does not match its label.
The paper's target notion: content held in a form the model could put into words if asked, as distinct from content it happens to be uttering. The top row is offered as an illustration of it.
The fixed token inventory of the model's tokenizer. The lens score distribution whose kurtosis defines κ is a distribution over this set.

numbers.meaning: The figure's layout. The paper says it shows three examples each of workspace-like features, motor features and low-kurtosis features; the caption assigns these to the top, middle and bottom rows. One passage of the prose instead refers to the low-κ examples as a "right column," so the exact arrangement is described inconsistently, but the grouping is the same either way.

The lens-kurtosis of the "numeric constraints and ranges" feature, the top-left card. It is the figure's worked example of a high-κ workspace feature, and the value is high because the feature's decoder direction loads almost entirely onto the lens vectors for a few tokens meaning "limit."
Where κ = 20.9 falls in the distribution of κ across all SAE features. The paper describes the distribution as heavy-tailed, so a value this high sits in its far tail.

The lens-kurtosis of two bottom-row examples: the decrementing for-loop variable feature and the markdown section header feature. A value this close to zero means the lens reads the direction almost as diffusely as a Gaussian score distribution, so the direction is not aligned with any small set of lens vectors.
The lens-kurtosis of the remaining bottom-row example, the feature for the first digit of a page range in an academic citation. Also effectively outside the J-space.
The excess kurtosis of a Gaussian, and therefore the reference point of the κ scale. Values near zero indicate a lens readout with no sharp peak.

numbers.value: top 10 lens tokens, more than 10% of the time
numbers.meaning: The threshold rule that classifies a high-κ feature as motor rather than workspace-like. Over the feature's strongest activations, if the actual next token appears among its ten most strongly expressed lens tokens on more than one occasion in ten, the paper calls it motor. The rule exists because motor and workspace features are indistinguishable on κ alone.
The number of top readout tokens printed for the "numeric constraints and ranges" feature: limits, 限, Limit, lím, limit. That five distinct tokens all express one meaning is the point being made.
